The '''stellated octahedron''', '''elevated octahedron''', or '''compound of two tetrahedra''' is a shape made from two [[regular tetrahedron|regular tetrahedra]] crossing each other. It is also called the '''stella octangula''' (Latin for "eight-pointed star"), a name given to it by [[Johannes Kepler]] in 1609, though it was known to earlier [[geometer]]s. It appears as a carving in a 13th century Turkish [[caravanserai]], and in modern architectural decorations; it has been depicted by [[Leonardo da Vinci]] in [[Pacioli]]'s 1509 ''[[Divina proportione|De Divina Proportione]]'', and in the works of [[M. C. Escher]].

The two tetrahedra of this shape form the simplest of the five regular [[polyhedral compound]]s, and the only regular polyhedral compound composed of only two polyhedra. They form the only fully symmetric [[stellation]]  of the [[Regular octahedron|octahedron]], and dually the only fully symmetric [[faceting]] of the [[cube]]. The combinatorial structure of this shape has been considered in multiple variations; these vary by whether the triangular faces of the two crossing tetrahedra are considered as faces themselves or whether they are subdivided into smaller triangular faces, and by whether interior boundaries or only the outer shell are included.

The [[stella octangula number]]s are [[figurate number]]s defined from the stellated octahedron. The two tetrahedra of a stellated octahedron can be extended to form a [[desmic system]] of three tetrahedra whose edges, extended to [[projective line]]s, each cross four other such lines. The stellated octahedron is the second stage of construction of a [[geode]]-like three-dimensional [[fractal]] within a cube, analogous to the two-dimensional [[Koch snowflake]]. The stellated octahedron can be generalized to compounds of two centrally symmetric [[simplex|simplices]] in any dimension, forming a family of shapes that also includes the two-dimensional [[hexagram]] or [[Star of David]]. Applications of the stellated octahedron include the fabrication of [[nanoparticle]]s with distinctive electromagnetic and biological properties, the theoretical understanding of [[quantum entanglement]], and the design of [[four-bar linkage]]s and [[auxetics|auxetic metamaterials]].

== Construction and properties ==
The stellated octahedron can be constructed in multiple different ways, including as a [[stellation]], as a [[compound polyhedron]], as a [[faceting]], and as an [[Augmentation (geometry)|augmentation]].

===Stellation===
[[File:Stellation of octahedron facets.svg|thumb|[[Stellation diagram]] of a stellated octahedron|alt=Three equilateral triangles meeting at three vertices]]
The stellated octahedron is constructed by a [[stellation]] of the [[regular octahedron]].<ref name=wenninger/><ref name=cdfp>{{citation
 | last1 = Coxeter | first1 = H. S. M.
 | last2 = Du Val | first2 = P.
 | last3 = Flather | first3 = H. T.
 | last4 = Petrie | first4 = J. F.
 | isbn = 0-387-90770-X
 | location = New York and Berlin
 | mr = 676126
 | page = 3
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | title = The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra
 | year = 1982}}</ref> In a stellation, the faces of the underlying polyhedron are extended within the same planes to enclose a different volume. It is generally required that the result maintain the same symmetry as the underlying polyhedron,<ref name=cdfp/> and with this restriction the stellated octahedron is the only stellation of the octahedron. Here, the extension in each plane consists of three equilateral triangles, surrounding the original triangular face of the octahedron and having the same size as it. These three triangles and the fourth triangle that they surround together form a larger equilateral triangle, and when constructed in this way, the stellated octahedron has eight of these larger equilateral triangle faces, crossing each other.<ref name=wenninger/><ref name=cdfp/>

Some versions of stellation also take the further step of removing parts of the extended faces to produce a polyhedral surface without self-crossings or interior voids.{{sfnp|Coxeter|Du Val|Flather|Petrie|1982|p=8}} For these versions, there are again eight faces, one in each plane, but each face takes the shape of an equilateral triangle with a hole formed by the removal of its [[midpoint triangle]]. This is shown in its [[stellation diagram]], which depicts the plane of a single extended face and shades the outer boundary of the stellation within that plane.<ref name=wenninger/>

===Compound===
The stellated octahedron is also a regular [[polyhedron compound]]. Here, a compound is a system of two or more polyhedra, and being regular means that it has symmetries that take every two vertices to each other, that take every two edges to each other, and that take every two faces to each other.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Smith | first = Anthony
 | date = February 1973
 | doi = 10.2307/3615168
 | issue = 399
 | journal = The Mathematical Gazette
 | jstor = 3615168
 | pages = 39–46
 | title = Some regular compounds of star-polyhedra
 | volume = 57}}</ref> The stellated compound is a compound of two [[regular tetrahedra]], related to each other by a [[central symmetry]] through the centroid of each tetrahedron. Hence, the stellated octahedron is also called the compound of two tetrahedra.<ref name=cdfp/>

Both tetrahedra can be inscribed in a cube, and each one shares four vertices with the cube.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Hilbert | first1=David | author1-link=David Hilbert | last2=Cohn-Vossen | first2=Stephan | author2-link=Stephan Cohn-Vossen | title=Geometry and the Imagination|title-link=Geometry and the Imagination | publisher=Chelsea | location=New York | edition=2nd | year=1952|pages=92–93}}</ref> The two tetrahedra share a common [[midsphere]], making the compound [[self-dual]].<ref name=pugh>{{citation
 | last = Pugh | first = Anthony
 | isbn = 9780520030565
 | page = 88
 | publisher = University of California Press
 | title = Polyhedra: A Visual Approach
 | year = 1976
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=IDDxpYQTR7kC&pg=PA88
}}</ref> The regular octahedron whose stellation forms this compound can be recovered as the intersection of the two tetrahedra.<ref name=barnes>{{citation
 | last = Barnes | first = John
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-05092-3
 | page = 253
 | publisher = Springer
 | title = Gems of Geometry
 | year = 2009
 | isbn = 978-3-642-05091-6
}}.</ref> This compound is related to several others: stellating the [[compound of five octahedra]] produces five stellated octahedra that together form the [[compound of ten tetrahedra]], and selecting one tetrahedron from each of these five stellated octahedra produces the [[compound of five tetrahedra]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|Du Val|Flather|Petrie|1982|p=4}}

If the edges of two congruent tetrahedra are arranged in this configuration, it is possible to slide the two tetrahedra against each other, to less symmetric configurations, in such a way that each pair of crossing edges remains [[coplanar]]. The relative positions of the two tetrahedra that can be reached in this way form a system of one- and two-dimensional [[smooth manifold]]s within the [[Configuration space (physics)#Rigid body in 3D space|six-dimensional configuration space]] of positions of one tetrahedron relative to the other.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Tarnai | first1 = T.
 | last2 = Makai | first2 = E.
 | doi = 10.1098/rspa.1989.0063
 | issue = 1865
 | journal = [[Proceedings of the Royal Society]]
 | jstor = 2398566
 | mr = 1007547
 | pages = 419–442
 | title = A movable pair of tetrahedra
 | volume = 423
 | year = 1989
 | bibcode = 1989RSPSA.423..419T
 }}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Zsombor-Murray | first1 = Paul J.
 | last2 = Hyder | first2 = Alexander
 | date = January 1992
 | doi = 10.1016/0921-8890(92)90040-6
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Robotics and Autonomous Systems
 | pages = 227–236
 | title = An equilateral tetrahedral mechanism
 | volume = 9}}</ref>

===Faceting===
[[File:CubeAndStel.svg|thumb|Stellated octahedron as a cube faceting|alt=Refer to caption]]
The stellated octahedron is a [[faceting]] of the [[cube]], meaning that it is a polyhedron or compound polyhedron within a cube that uses only the vertices of the cube. Faceting is the [[dual polyhedron|dual]] process to stellation.
For the faceting that produces the stellated octahedron, the edges of the faceting are the [[face diagonal]]s of the cube, and the faces are equilateral triangles connecting the three neighbors of each cube vertex. These vertices, edges, and faces form two tetrahedra, forming the stellated octahedron as a compound of two tetrahedra.<ref name=inchbald/>

Although the cube can be faceted in multiple ways with lesser symmetry, the stellated octahedron is the only faceting that has the same [[Point groups in three dimensions|three-dimensional point group symmetry]] as the cube,<ref name=inchbald>{{citation
 | last = Inchbald | first = Guy
 | year = 2006
 | title = Facetting diagrams
 | journal = [[The Mathematical Gazette]]
 | volume = 90 | issue = 518 | pages = 253&ndash;261
 | doi = 10.1017/S0025557200179653
 | jstor = 40378613
}}</ref> an [[octahedral symmetry]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|1973|p=[http://books.google.com/books?id=2ee7AQAAQBAJ&pg=PA49 49]}}<ref name=smith>{{citation
 | last = Smith | first = James
 | year = 2000
 | title = Methods of Geometry
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=B0khWEZmOlwC&pg=PA403
 | page = 403&ndash;404
 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons
 | isbn = 978-1-118-03103-2
}}</ref>

===Augmentation===
[[File:Diamant1.gif|thumb|The [[triakis octahedron]], a [[convex polyhedron]] with the same combinatorial structure as the outer boundary of the augmented octahedron|alt=Rotating triakis octahedron]]
A shape with the same surface geometry as the stellated octahedron, but with a different combinatorial face structure, can be obtained as an [[augmentation (geometry)|augmentation]] of the regular octahedron, by adding tetrahedral [[Pyramid (geometry)|pyramids]] on each face. In this form, the faces of the augmented octahedron are equilateral triangles, of half the side length and one quarter the area of the faces of the corresponding compound of two tetrahedra.<ref name=trigg/> The volume of the augmented octahedron is the sum of the volumes of eight tetrahedra and one regular octahedron. For an augmented octahedron with edge {{nowrap|length <math>a</math>,}} this gives volume
<math display=block>V=8\frac{a^3\sqrt2}{12}+\frac{a^3\sqrt2}{3}=a^3\sqrt2.</math>
Equivalently, the volume is 3/2 of the volume of one of the larger tetrahedra forming it as a compound of two tetrahedra, and 1/2 of the volume of the cube in which it is inscribed.<ref name=loeb>{{citation
 | last = Loeb | first = Arthur | author-link = Arthur Lee Loeb
 | editor-first = Jean-François | editor-last = Gabriel
 | title = Beyond the Cube: The Architecture of Space Frames and Polyhedra
 | contribution = Deconstruction of the cube
 | contribution-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=FkM0945nFV8C&pg=PA233
 | page = 233
 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons
 | year = 1997
}}</ref>

When only the outer faces of the added pyramids are used, this construction produces a non-convex polyhedron with the same combinatorial structure as the convex [[triakis octahedron]], a [[Catalan solid]] with much shorter pyramids. Any of these pyramid attachments, convex or non-convex, may be known as the [[Kleetope]] of an octahedron.<ref name=bpv>{{citation
 | last1 = Brigaglia | first1 = Aldo
 | last2 = Palladino | first2 = Nicla
 | last3 = Vaccaro | first3 = Maria Alessandra
 | editor1-last = Emmer | editor1-first = Michele
 | editor2-last = Abate | editor2-first = Marco
 | contribution = Historical notes on star geometry in mathematics, art and nature
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-93949-0_17
 | pages = 197–211
 | publisher = Springer International Publishing
 | title = Imagine Math 6: Between Culture and Mathematics
 | year = 2018| hdl = 10447/325250
 | isbn = 978-3-319-93948-3
 | hdl-access = free
 }}</ref> For another choice of pyramid height, intermediate between the triakis octahedron and stellated octahedron, pairs of adjacent triangle faces from different pyramids lie on the same plane, and the shape [[degeneracy (mathematics)|degenerates]] to the [[rhombic dodecahedron]].<ref>{{citation |last=Loeb |first=Arthur L.|author-link=Arthur Lee Loeb |year=1991 |title=Space Structures: Their Harmony and Counterpoint |pages=137 |place=Boston, Massachusetts |publisher=Birkhäuser |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-0437-4 |isbn=978-1-4612-6759-1}}</ref>

{{Anchor|Stellated octahedron graph}}The outer shell of the augmented octahedron, with 24 equilateral-triangle faces, is an example of a [[Deltahedron#Non-convex deltahedron|non-convex deltahedron]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Pedersen | first1 = M. C.
 | last2 = Hyde | first2 = S. T.
 | title = Polyhedra and packings from hyperbolic honeycombs
 | year = 2018
 | volume = 115 | issue = 27 | pages = 6905–6910
 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1720307115
 | journal = [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]
 | doi-access = free
 | pmid = 29925600
 | pmc = 6142264
 | bibcode = 2018PNAS..115.6905P
}}</ref><ref name=trigg>{{citation
 | last = Trigg | first = Charles W. | author-link = Charles W. Trigg
 | doi = 10.1080/0025570X.1978.11976675
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Mathematics Magazine]]
 | jstor = 2689647
 | mr = 1572246
 | pages = 55–57
 | title = An infinite class of deltahedra
 | volume = 51
 | year = 1978}}</ref> There are several different ways of arranging the 24 equilateral triangles of this shape into a [[Net (polyhedron)|net]], a planar system of polygons from which this deltahedron can be folded.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Roelofs | first = Rinus
 | editor1-last = Holdener | editor1-first = Judy
 | editor2-last = Torrence | editor2-first = Eve
 | editor3-last = Fong | editor3-first = Chamberlain
 | editor4-last = Seaton | editor4-first = Katherine
 | contribution = What if Albrecht Dürer had unfolded Leonardo da Vinci's elevated polyhedra?
 | contribution-url = https://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2023/bridges2023-321.html
 | isbn = 978-1-938664-45-8
 | location = Phoenix, Arizona
 | pages = 321–328
 | publisher = Tessellations Publishing
 | title = Proceedings of Bridges 2023: Mathematics, Art, Music, Architecture, Culture
 | year = 2023}}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Cundy | first1 = H. Martyn | author1-link = Martyn Cundy
 | last2 = Rollett | first2 = A. P.
 | edition = 2nd
 | location = Oxford
 | mr = 0124167
 | contribution = 3.10.1 Stella octangula (two tetrahedra)
 | page = 129
 | publisher = Clarendon Press
 | title = Mathematical Models
 | title-link = Mathematical Models (Cundy and Rollett)
 | year = 1961}}</ref> When the faces of the inner octahedron are retained rather than replaced, the resulting structure (the ''elevation'' of the octahedron) has 32 equilateral triangles in two shells: the outer augmentation and an inner regular octahedron. Its [[vertex figure]] at the inner six vertices takes the form of two nested polygons, a square within an octagon.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Roelofs | first = Rinus
 | editor1-last = Torrence | editor1-first = Eve
 | editor2-last = Torrence | editor2-first = Bruce
 | editor3-last = Séquin | editor3-first = Carlo
 | editor4-last = McKenna | editor4-first = Douglas
 | editor5-last = Fenyvesi | editor5-first = Kristóf
 | editor6-last = Sarhangi | editor6-first = Reza
 | contribution = The elevation of Coxeter's infinite regular polyhedron 444444
 | contribution-url = https://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2016/bridges2016-33.html
 | isbn = 978-1-938664-19-9
 | location = Phoenix, Arizona
 | pages = 33–40
 | publisher = Tessellations Publishing
 | title = Proceedings of Bridges 2016: Mathematics, Music, Art, Architecture, Education, Culture
 | year = 2016}}</ref> The [[undirected graph]] obtained from the augmented octahedron, with or without its eight inner triangles, has 14 [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] and 36 [[edge (graph theory)|edges]]; it has been called the ''stellated octahedron graph''.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Liu | first = Shihao
 | editor1-last = Hillel | editor1-first = Eshcar
 | editor2-last = Palmieri | editor2-first = Roberto
 | editor3-last = Rivière | editor3-first = Etienne
 | contribution = The impossibility of approximate agreement on a larger class of graphs
 | doi = 10.4230/LIPICS.OPODIS.2022.22
 | pages = 22:1–22:20
 | publisher = Schloss Dagstuhl – Leibniz-Zentrum für Informatik
 | series = LIPIcs
 | title = 26th International Conference on Principles of Distributed Systems, OPODIS 2022, Brussels, Belgium, December 13–15, 2022
 | volume = 253
 | year = 2022
 | doi-access = free
 | isbn = 978-3-95977-265-5
 }}; see page 22:13</ref>

As an augmented polyhedron, the stellated octahedron has two [[dihedral angle]]s between two equilateral triangles, namely a convex and a concave angle, obtained from the angle of a tetrahedron and an octahedron. The stellated octahedron's convex angle is the same as the dihedral angle of a tetrahedron, whereas its concave angle is the sum of two tetrahedra attached to an octahedron. That is,<ref>{{citation|last=McCooey|first=David I.|title=Stella Octangula (Surface) |url=https://dmccooey.com/polyhedra/StellaOctangula2.html|website=dmccooey.com}}.</ref>
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
 \arccos\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) &\approx 70.5^\circ, \\
 \arccos\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) + 2 \arccos\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) &\approx 250.5^\circ.
\end{align}</math>

== Appearances ==
===Historical===
{{multiple image
 | image1 = De divina proportione - Illustration 22.jpg
 | caption1 = [[Luca Pacioli]] 1509's ''[[Divina proportione]]'' introduced the concept of the elevation by attaching pyramids to an octahedron
 | alt1 = Page of Divina proportione showing a stellated octahedron
 | image2 = Perspectiva Corporum Regularium 32a.jpg
 | caption2 =  A stellated octahedron in ''[[Perspectiva corporum regularium]]'' (1568)
 | alt2 = Skeletal drawing of a stellated octahedron
 | image3 = Gérard Douffet, Visite du pape Nicolas V au tombeau de saint François d'Assise, 1627 (huile sur toile ; 450 × 400 cm, Munich, Alte Pinakothek).jpg
 | alt3 = Painting of various activities in a church chapel; a skeletal stellated octahedron hangs from the dome above
 | caption3 = [[Gérard Douffet]], ''Pope Nicholas V's visit to the tomb of Saint Francis of Assisi'' (1627)
 | total_width = 540
}}
One of the geometric stone carvings in the {{ill|Sahib Ata (İshaklı) caravanserai|tr|İshaklı Kervansarayı}}, built in the 13th century in [[Sultandağı]], [[Turkey]], takes the shape of a stellated octahedron.<ref>{{citation |last1=Hisarligil |first1=Hakan |last2=Bolak Hisarligil |first2=Beyhan |year=2018 |title=The geometry of cuboctahedra in Medieval art in Anatolia |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00004-017-0363-7 |journal=Nexus Network Journal |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=125–152 |doi=10.1007/s00004-017-0363-7 |issn=1590-5896}}</ref>

[[Luca Pacioli]] 1509's ''[[Divina proportione]]'' introduced the concept of the elevation of a polyhedron, formed by replacing each face of the polyhedron by a [[pyramid]]. Pacioli describes the elevated octahedron (named by him in Latin, {{lang|la|octaedron elevatum}}) as having two layers of faces, the outer visible layer having 24 equilateral triangles and the hidden inner layer taking the form of an octahedron with another 8 equilateral triangle faces. [[Leonardo da Vinci]]'s illustration of an elevated regular octahedron for the book takes the form of a stellated octahedron.<ref name="roelofs"/>

The stellated octahedron subsequently appeared in Renaissance books of illustrated polyhedra including Lorenz Stöer's ''Geometria et Perspectiva'' (1567),<ref>{{citation

 | publisher = Springer Nature Switzerland
 | title = Beyond Digital Representation: Advanced Experiences in AR and AI for Cultural Heritage and Innovative Design}}</ref> [[Daniele Barbaro]]'s ''La pratica della perspettiva'' (1568),<ref>{{citation

 | last = Cromwell | first = Peter R.

 | isbn = 978-0-521-55432-9

}}</ref> The stellated octahedron was rediscovered as a [[faceting]] of the cube by Frans Cophart of the [[Collegium Musicum]] in [[Leiden]]; Cophart claimed that this was a sixth regular polyhedron, because its 24 faces were both regular and symmetric. [[Simon Stevin]] disagreed in his 1583 work ''Problemata geometrica'', noting that Cophart's shape had two kinds of vertices, instead of all vertices being symmetric to each other.<ref name=bpv/><ref>{{citation|title=Principal Works of Simon Stevin: Mathematics|year=1955|publisher=C.V. Swets & Zeitlinger|url=https://www.vliz.be/imisdocs/publications/ocrd/213986.pdf|page=127|editor1-first=Ernst|editor1-last=Crone|editor2-first=E. J.|editor2-last=Dijksterhuis|editor3-first=R. J.|editor3-last=Forbes|editor4-first=M. G. J.|editor4-last=Minnaert|editor5-first=A.|editor5-last=Pannekoek}}</ref> [[Johannes Kepler]] in his 1609's ''[[Harmonice Mundi]]'' introduced the concept of [[stellation]], the extension of the faces of one polyhedron within the same planes to form a different polyhedron, and named the stellated octahedron the "stella octangula", Latin for "eight-pointed star".<ref name="roelofs">{{citation

A 1627 painting by [[Gérard Douffet]], ''Pope Nicholas V's visit to the tomb of Saint Francis of Assisi'', depicts a stellated octahedron hanging from the dome of the church above the tomb, over a scene of an [[exorcism]]. Art historian Pierre-Yves Kairis calls out this detail as a "[[Mannerism|Mannerist]] oddity".<ref>{{citation|title=Le peintre Gérard Douffet, fondateur de l'école liégeoise du XVIIe siècle|first=Pierre-Yves|last=Kairis|journal=Bulletins de l'Académie Royale de Belgique|year=1988|volume=70|pages=40–54|url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/barb_0378-0716_1988_num_70_1_41157|language=fr}}. See p. 47: "Sans doute faut-il compter au nombre des étrangetés maniéristes
la mystérieuse étoile en relief formée de deux tétraèdres réguliers emboîtés et apparemment suspendue dans le vide au-dessus de la scène d'exorcisme."</ref>

===In science and technology===
[[File:3D model of a Stellated Octahedron.stl|thumb|3D model of stellated octahedron|alt=Refer to caption]]
Researchers have used various methods to fabricate [[nanoparticle]]s of [[gold]] and [[palladium]] with the "octopod" shape of a stellated octahedron. The pointed shapes of these particles give them distinctive electromagnetic and biological properties.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Chang | first1 = Yi-Xin
 | last2 = Gao | first2 = Hui-Min
 | last3 = Zhang | first3 = Ning-Ning
 | last4 = Tao | first4 = Xing-Fu
 | last5 = Sun | first5 = Tianmeng
 | last6 = Zhang | first6 = Junhu
 | last7 = Lu | first7 = Zhong-Yuan
 | last8 = Liu | first8 = Kun
 | last9 = Yang | first9 = Bai
 | date = August 2018
 | doi = 10.3389/fchem.2018.00335
 | journal = [[Frontiers in Chemistry]]
 | title = Synergistic reducing effect for synthesis of well-defined Au nanooctopods with ultra-narrow plasmon band width and high photothermal conversion efficiency

The stellated octahedron has also been used in [[quantum mechanics]]. The [[Bell state]]s of two [[qubit]]s can be modeled as the four vertices of a [[tetrahedron]], consisting of all possible states of the two qubits. A "Peres transformation", the reflection of this tetrahedron, forms a second tetrahedron, crossing the first one to form a stellated octahedron, within which the central octahedron formed by the intersection of the two tetrahedra forms the set of Bell-diagonal [[separable states]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Aravind | first = P. K.
 | date = August 1997
 | doi = 10.1016/s0375-9601(97)00438-6
 | issue = 1–2
 | journal = [[Physics Letters A]]
 | pages = 7–10
 | title = The "twirl", stella octangula and mixed state entanglement
 | volume = 233
 | bibcode = 1997PhLA..233....7A
 }}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Ericsson | first = Åsa
 | date = April 2002
 | doi = 10.1016/s0375-9601(02)00181-0
 | issue = 5–6
 | journal = [[Physics Letters A]]
 | pages = 256–258
 | title = Separability and the stella octangula
 | volume = 295
 | arxiv = quant-ph/0109099
 | bibcode = 2002PhLA..295..256E
 }}</ref>

In the design of [[mechanical linkage]]s, the design space of a planar [[four-bar linkage]] can be studied by normalizing the length of a fixed bar to one, and defining parameters for the lengths of the other three bars. The tangents of the angles made at the two ends of the fixed bar are then related by a [[quartic equation]] whose coefficients involve pairwise products of eight linear combinations of the length parameters. The eight planes in the parameter space where these eight combinations become zero form the faces of a stellated octahedron. A similar analysis, producing a shape resembling a stellated octahedron but with curved surfaces, applies to spherical four-bar linkages.<ref>{{citation
 | first1 = M. John D. | last1 = Hayes
 | first2 = Mirja | last2 = Rotzoll
 | first3 = Colin | last3 = Ingalls
 | first4 = Martin | last4 = Pfurner
 | contribution = Design parameter space of spherical four-bar linkages
 | pages = 19–27
 | title = New Trends in Mechanism and Machine Science: Proceedings of the 8th European Conference on Mechanism Science (EuCoMeS) 
 | series = Mechanisms and Machine Science 
 | volume = 89
 | publisher = Springer Cham
 | year = 2020
 | editor-first1 = Doina | editor-last1 = Pisla
 | editor-first2 = Burkhard | editor-last2 = Corves
 | editor-first3 = Calin | editor-last3 = Vaida
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-030-55061-5_3
 | isbn = 978-3-030-55060-8
 | contribution-url = https://www.academia.edu/download/96376269/DPS-Spherical4R-RevF.pdf}}</ref>

Tanaka et al have investigated [[auxetics|auxetic metamaterials]] in which stretching the material in one direction does not necessarily cause compression in perpendicular directions, obtained by repeating a three-dimensional grid of unit cells, each taking the form of a stellated octahedron whose eight rigid tetrahedra are connected to some but not all neighboring tetrahedra at hinged joints.<ref>{{citation |last1=Tanaka |first1=H. |title=Primitive rotation mechanism of periodic stellated octahedron units with sharing edges |journal=International Journal of Solids and Structures |volume=185–186 |pages=485–499 |year=2020 |doi=10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2019.09.013 |last2=Suga |first2=K. |last3=Shibutani |first3=Y.}}</ref>

Investigation of [[granular material]]s with particles in the shape of stellated octahedra found them to have an [[angle of repose]] intermediate between the shallower angles of convex particles with a shape closer to spheres and the steeper angles of tetrahedra and more extremely non-convex [[caltrop]]-shaped particles.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Landauer | first1 = Johann
 | last2 = Kuhn | first2 = Michael
 | last3 = Nasato | first3 = Daniel S.
 | last4 = Foerst | first4 = Petra
 | last5 = Briesen | first5 = Heiko
 | date = February 2020
 | doi = 10.1016/j.powtec.2019.11.051
 | journal = Powder Technology
 | pages = 711–718
 | title = Particle shape matters – Using 3D printed particles to investigate fundamental particle and packing properties
 | volume = 361}}</ref>

Il s'agit d'une projection du sceau de Salamon dans l'espace à trois dimensions.}}</ref> French historian Henri Calhiol has documented stone carvings of this shape on several country houses in the [[Arrondissement of Mirande]] of southwestern France.<ref>{{citation|url=https://lejournaldugers.fr/index.php/article/83896-tout-savoir-sur-les-octaedres-dans-le-gers|language=fr|title=Tout savoir sur les octaèdres dans le Gers : Henri Calhiol vous dévoile leur mystère|date=May 10, 2025|newspaper=Le journal du Gers|access-date=2026-06-29}}</ref> They appear also in interior wooden staircase carvings in the [[Maison du Val de Villé]] in northeastern France.<ref name=vdv>{{citation|url=https://musee-valleedeville.com/loctaedre-regulier-etoile/|title=L’octaèdre régulier étoilé|work=La thématique du moment|year=2024|publisher=Maison du Val de Villé|language=fr|access-date=2026-07-04}}</ref>

===Mysticism===

Some modern mystics have associated this shape with the "merkaba":<ref>{{citation|title=Sedona: Beyond the Vortex: Activating the Planetary Ascension Program with Sacred Geometry, the Vortex, and the Merkaba|first=Richard|last=Dannelley|publisher=Light Technology Publishing|year=1995|isbn=9781622336708|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eMDBS8SNUp8C&pg=PT14|page=14}}</ref> a "counterrotating field of light"<ref name="DMelchizedek">{{citation|title=The Ancient Secret of the Flower of Life: An Edited Transcript of the Flower of Life Workshop Presented Live to Mother Earth from 1985 to 1994 -, Volume 1|first=Drunvalo|last=Melchizedek|publisher=Light Technology Publishing|year=2000|isbn=9781891824173|page=4,5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E0FEcoK0ds4C&pg=PA4}}</ref>{{efn|1=Specifically, Melchizedek describes the merkaba as made of two coincidental stellated octahedra, or "star tetrahedra" that counter-rotate with respect to each other<ref>{{citation |author-last=Melchizedek |author-first=Drunvalo |title=The Teaching On Spherical Breathing (Merkaba Meditation) |url=https://archive.org/stream/DrunvaloMelchizedekMerkabaMeditation_201810/Drunvalo%20Melchizedek%20-%20Merkaba%20Meditation_djvu.txt |website=[[Internet Archive]] |date=26 Dec 1994 }}</ref> (i.e., four tetrahedra total, in the form of two [[self-dual]] stellated octahedra).}} that "transport[s] body and soul to other dimensions."<ref>{{citation |last=Marar |first=Ton |chapter=Ancient Greek big bang theory |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-07442-4_2 |title=A Ludic Journey into Geometric Topology |publisher=[[Springer Nature]] |location=Cham |pages=25 |date=May 20, 2022 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-07442-4 |isbn=978-3-031-07441-7 |mr=4485665 }}</ref> [[New Age]] authors have attributed the merkaba to ancient Egyptian origins<ref name="DMelchizedek" /> — traditionally, "mer" stood for [[pyramid]], "[[Ancient Egyptian conception of the soul|ka]]" for [[soul]], and "[[Ancient Egyptian conception of the soul#Ba (personality)|ba]]" for personality or spiritual essence that guides the soul. In a different tradition, Jewish [[Merkabah mysticism|"Merkabah" mysticism]] details a living ''chariot'' in the visions of [[Ezekiel]] (in Hebrew, [[chariot]] is written '''מֶרְכָּבָה''' and pronounced ''merkābâ'', where "rakab" means "to ride" or "to be carried"), used by higher angels for motility.<ref>{{citation|title=Pocket Dictionary of Biblical Studies: Over 300 Terms Clearly & Concisely Defined|series=The IVP Pocket Reference Series|first1=Arthur G.|last1=Patzia|first2=Anthony J.|last2=Petrotta|publisher=InterVarsity Press|year=2010|isbn=9780830867028|page=78|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=btEJAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA78}}</ref>

The triangles in the stellated octahedron have been used as a sign of the Christian [[Trinity]], copied 24 times for the 24 hours of the day.<ref name=vdv/> The resemblance between this shape and the two-dimensional [[star of David]] has also been frequently noted.<ref name=brisson>{{citation|title=Hypergraphics: Visualizing Complex Relationships in Art, Science, and Technology|first=David W.|last=Brisson|publisher=Westview Press for the American Association for the Advancement of Science|year=1978|page=220|quote=The Stella octangula is the 3-d analog of the Star of David}}</ref>

==Related concepts==
[[File:StellaOctangulaNumber.jpg|thumb|124 [[Neodymium magnet toys|magnetic balls]] arranged into the shape of a stellated octahedron|alt=A stellated octahedron made from magnetic balls sits on a bed of tiny green plants]]
===Stella octangula numbers===
{{main|Stella octangula number}}
The [[stella octangula number]]s are [[figurate number]]s that count the number of balls that can be arranged into the shape of a stellated octahedron. These numbers are the form of <math> n(2n^2 - 1) </math> for <math> n </math> being the positive integers; the first ten such numbers are:<ref name=cg>{{citation|title=The Book of Numbers|page=51|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0--3rcO7dMYC&pg=PA51|first1=John|last1=Conway|author1-link=John Horton Conway|first2=Richard|last2=Guy|author2-link=Richard K. Guy|publisher=Springer|year=1996|isbn=978-0-387-97993-9}}</ref>
:0, 1, 14, 51, 124, 245, 426, 679, 1016, 1449, 1990, .... {{OEIS|A007588}}.
The only two of these numbers that are also [[square number]]s are 1 and<ref>{{citation|url=https://homepages.warwick.ac.uk/staff/S.Siksek/papers/phdnew.pdf|first=Samir|last=Siksek|type=Ph.D. thesis|publisher=University of Exeter|year=1995|title=Descents on Curves of Genus I|pages=16–17}}</ref> <math display=block>9\,653\,449 = 3107^2 = 169(2\cdot 169^2-1).</math>

===Tangent circles===
[[File:Stella octangula circle packing.svg|thumb|Eight circles that, when lifted to a sphere by [[stereographic projection]], lie on the face planes of a stellated octahedron|alt=Pattern of eight tangent circles]]
It is a theorem of [[absolute geometry]] that, when [[Descartes' theorem|four circles are mutually tangent]], then there exists another set of four mutually tangent circles each crossing at right angles through three of the six points of tangency of the first four circles. When these circles all lie on a sphere, the planes through them form a compound of two tetrahedra, with the same combinatorial structure (but not necessarily the same shape) as a compound of two regular tetrahedra. In this case, the sphere that contains the circles is the [[midsphere]] of both tetrahedra.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Coxeter | first = H. S. M. | author-link = Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter
 | editor1-last = Prékopa | editor1-first = András

 | contribution = An absolute property of four mutually tangent circles
 | doi = 10.1007/0-387-29555-0_5
 | isbn = 978-0387-29554-1
 | location = New York
 | mr = 2191243
 | pages = 109–114
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Mathematics and Its Applications
 | title = Non-Euclidean Geometries: János Bolyai memorial volume, Papers from the International Conference on Hyperbolic Geometry held in Budapest, July 6–12, 2002
 | volume = 581
 | year = 2006}}</ref>

===Fractal===
[[File:01 3D Koch Schneeflocke-5.svg|thumb|The third stage of construction of a three-dimensional [[fractal]] analogous to the [[Koch snowflake]]. The green triangles outline a central tetrahedron, the first stage, and the red triangles outline a second tetrahedron that in the second stage forms a stellated octahedron. The yellow and blue triangles are added in the third stage.|alt=Cube containing a fractal whose base form is a stellated octahedron]]
The [[Koch snowflake]], a two-dimensional [[fractal]] resembling a hexagram, can be generalized in three dimensions to a fractal whose first stage of construction is a [[regular tetrahedron]]. Each successive stage subdivides each triangle of the previous stage into four smaller equilateral triangles and then attaches a triangular pyramid to the middle triangle of each subdivided triangle. The second stage is a stellated octahedron. In the limit, the outer surface of this three-dimensional fractal forms a [[cube]], but unlike a cube it has a [[geode]]-like interior fractal structure.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Goodwin | first = P.
 | date = October 1985
 | doi = 10.2307/3617525
 | issue = 449

 | jstor = 3617525

 | title = A polyhedral series or two
 | volume = 69}}</ref><ref>{{citation

 | volume = 10

===Desmic tetrahedra===
{{main|Desmic system}}
The two tetrahedra of the compound view of the stellated octahedron are "desmic", meaning that (when extended into a line in [[projective space]]) each edge of one tetrahedron crosses two opposite edges of the other tetrahedron. One of these two crossings is visible in the stellated octahedron; the other crossing occurs at a [[point at infinity]] of the projective space, where each edge of one tetrahedron crosses the parallel edge of the other tetrahedron. These two tetrahedra can be completed to a [[desmic system]] of three tetrahedra, where the third tetrahedron has as its four vertices the four [[center of perspectivity|centers of perspectivity]] of the first two tetrahedra: three points at infinity (the three points where [[parallel line]]s extending the edges of its enclosing cube meet) and the centroid of the two finite tetrahedra. Every desmic system is equivalent under [[projective transformation]]s to a system formed from a stellated octahedron in this way.<ref>{{citation | authorlink=R. W. H. T. Hudson | last1=Hudson | first1=R. W. H. T. | title=Kummer's quartic surface | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=1905|url=https://archive.org/details/kummersquartics00hudsgoog
|pages=1–2}}</ref> The same twelve tetrahedron vertices also form the points of [[Reye's configuration]].<ref>{{Citation | last1=Hilbert | first1=David | author1-link=David Hilbert | last2=Cohn-Vossen | first2=Stephan | author2-link=Stephan Cohn-Vossen | title=Geometry and the Imagination | publisher=Chelsea | location=New York | edition=2nd | year=1952|contribution=22. Reye's configuration|pages=134–143}}</ref>

===In other dimensions===
This shape can be seen as a 3D extension of the [[hexagram]]:<ref name=brisson/> the hexagram is a two-dimensional shape formed from two crossing equilateral triangles, [[central symmetry|centrally symmetric]] to each other, and in the same way, the stellated octahedron can be formed from two centrally symmetric crossing tetrahedra. This can be generalized to any desired number of higher dimensions; the four-dimensional equivalent construction is the [[compound of two 5-cells]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Schoenberg | first = I. J. | author-link = Isaac Jacob Schoenberg
 | issue = 1–3
 | journal = Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica
 | mr = 645535
 | pages = 273–292
 | title = Extremum problems for the motions of a billiard ball. IV. A higher-dimensional analogue of Kepler's Stella Octangula
 | url = https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA086550.pdf
 | volume = 14
 | year = 1979
}}.</ref>
